newsitem.title: USA: Big oil firms call MMS oil royalty plan unlawful.
newsitem.headline: Big oil firms call MMS oil royalty plan unlawful.

text.p: The American Petroleum Institute on Tuesday accused the Minerals Management Service of attempting to make an illegal change in the way oil royalties are calculated.

In a letter accompanying comments on a proposed rule by the Interior Department agency that could make producers pay higher royalties for oil produced on federal lands, API said the plan posed "major problems at several levels."
"In a nutshell, the MMS Proposal for valuation of crude oil is too costly, does not work and exceeds the MMS' statutory authority," API General Counsel William Frick wrote in the May 27 letter.

"Moreover, the rulemaking process employed is rife with procedural problems and draws the MMS' energy away from real solutions, namely, revision of the existing regulations and/or development of a viable royalty-in-kind program," Frick added.

MMS proposed in January to stop basing royalty calculations on companies' posted prices for crude oil at the lease, which it said undervalued oil, and instead base calculations on NYMEX futures and Alaskan oil prices.
Comments on the plan are due on Wednesday.

"Not only would the Proposal unlawfully lead to a value different than the value of production at the lease, but it attempts to 'clarify' that the lessee's existing duty to place production in marketable condition also includes the duty to market free of charge to the lessor," the letter said.
The API said that the administrative hassle of using the new method of calculating royalties was "wholly out of proportion to its purported benefits."

An API spokesman said that despite the accusation the MMS was going beyond its legal authority, it was too early to say whether the industry would sue the agency if it went ahead with the new oil valuation plan.
"It would be premature to say we're going to sue," API spokesman Joe Lastelic said.

However, according to a letter released on Tuesday by a government watchdog group, Project on Government Oversight, the oil industry may be planning to use whatever tactics necessary to hold up the new regulations.

The letter, written on February 26 and released by the watchdog group, allegedly written by Pat Holloway of Phoenix Horizontal in Giddings, Texas to Assistant Secretary of the Interior Bob Armstrong, described an oil industry meeting held to discuss opposition to the rules.

Independent Petroleum Association of America staff confirmed that such a meeting was held on February 20 with members of IPAA and API. The IPAA said it could not immediately provide any further details.

"The strategy discussed at the meeting was to seek to delay the proposed regulations as long as possible, and then file suit in the name of the IPAA ... to prevent them from becoming effective on whatever procedural (not substantive) grounds are available," the letter claimed.

"It was suggested that the IPAA-API should consult with the tobacco industry on legal tactics, since that industry has so much more experience in litigating against government regulations than the oil industry," it said.
Holloway refused to confirm that he had written the letter. "I really couldn't confirm that I've written Bob Armstrong at all," he said, before hanging up on a reporter.

A spokesman for Armstrong also declined to confirm or deny whether Armstrong had received such a letter, saying that the copy released by the Project on Government Oversight watchdog group with some sections blacked out could not be authenticated.
"If someone wants to know if we got a letter that said all of that, then you need to request it through FOIA (the Freedom of Information Act)," said Minerals Management Service spokeswoman A.B. Wade.
